newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada's Martin says tax cut could boost rates.
newsitem.headline: Canada's Martin says tax cut could boost rates.

text.p: Canadian Finance Minister Paul Martin said on Thursday that a broad-based tax cut could slow the reduction of Canada's deficit and lead to higher interest rates.

"It is my belief that anything that would slow up the deficit fight will have an impact on interest rates. There is no greater bang for the buck that we can deliver to the economy and to job creation than, in fact, to get those interest rates down," Martin told a Nesbitt Burns conference call.
He said, however, that the government could introduce selective tax cuts while still trying to balance the budget.
"I think that we can, in the interim, proceed with selective tax cuts," Martin said.

"I think that we can do that immediately and we will do so," he added. "We would certainly hope to bring down unemployment insurance premiums as fast as would be fiscally responsible. When you look at the government's revenue, that also amounts to a tax cut."
He said that in his last budget he introduced tax cuts or tax credits for education and caregiving.
Martin said Canada's tax system was "unduly complex" and voiced hope that tax reform would be a priority in the coming years.
"There is no doubt that I would hope that one of the main priorities in the next mandate would be tax reform," he said.

In a budget update Wednesday, Martin said he beat his C$32.7 billion deficit target for 1995/96 by C$4.1 billion and was on target to meet or exceed his targets for 1996/97 and 1997/98. He also set a deficit target of C$9 billion or 1.0 percent of gross domestic product for 1998/99. But he said a broad-based tax cut before Canada balanced its books would be irresponsible.
-- Malina Poshtova Zang, Reuters Ottawa Bureau (613) 235-6745
